title: Enhanced Electrochemical CO2 Reduction of Cu@CuxO Nanoparticles Decorated on 3D Vertical Graphene with Intrinsic sp3‐type Defect
abstract: Defective 3D vertical graphene (VG) with a relatively large surface area, high defect density, and increased surface electrons is synthesized via a scalable plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition method, together with a postsynthesis Ar-plasma treatment (VG-Ar). Subsequently, Cu@CuxO nanoparticles are deposited onto VG-Ar (Cu/VG-Ar) through a galvanostatic pulsed electrodeposition method. These Cu@CuxO nanocatalyst systems exhibit a superior electrochemical CO2 reduction performance when compared to Cu-based catalysts supported on commercial graphene paper or pristine VG without postsynthesis Ar-plasma treatment. The Cu/VG-Ar achieves the highest CO2 reduction Faradaic efficiency of 60.6% (83.5% of which are attributed to liquid products, i.e., formate, ethanol, and n-propanol) with a 5.6 mA cm−2 partial current density at −1.2 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). The improved CO2 reduction performance of Cu/VG-Ar originates from the well-dispersed Cu@CuxO nanoparticles deposited on the defective VG-Ar. The intrinsic carbon defects on VG-Ar can suppress the hydrogen evolution reaction as well as tune the interaction between VG and Cu@CuxO, thus impeding the excessive oxidation of Cu2O species deposited on VG-Ar. The defective VG-Ar and stabilized Cu@CuxO enhances CO2 adsorption and promotes electron transfer to the adsorbed CO2 and intermediates on the catalyst surface, thus improving the overall CO2 reduction performance.

The decreased costs of electricity generation from renewable sources (e.g., solar energy and wind energy) make the renewable energy more affordable.[2] Hence, the renewable-powered electrochemical (EC) CO2 reduction, which could convert CO2 to value-added fuel products with high selectivity and rapid electron transfer kinetics, has become a promising alternative for CO2 utilization.[3] However, using costly noble metal catalysts (e.g., Pt, Au, and Pd) in the EC CO2 reduction process has become a major setback for its commercialization, and therefore necessitates the development of a more economical catalyst option.[4]

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Global warming due to the increasing CO2 emissions from the consumption of fossil fuels has become one of the most severe

i-propanol etc.,).[5] However, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is highly competitive during EC CO2 reduction when using the Cu-based electrode due to its lower energy barrier and higher reaction kinetics, lowering its Faradaic efficiency (FE) toward CO2 conversion.[6] Numerous researchers have focused on the design of Cu-based electrodes to increase their CO2 reduction FE. For instance, Li and Kanan reported a series of Cu electrodes with surface nanorods prepared through electrochemical reduction of Cu foils with Cu2O layers.[7] The research showed that Cu surfaces with particle or grain boundary structures formed from the electroreduction of the thicker Cu2O layer with larger surface area favored the formation of CO2•− intermediate and suppressed HER. Appel also confirmed that nanostructured Cu electrodes with small crystals exhibited improved EC CO2 reduction performance.[8] In agreement with these studies, Flake and Mikosch reported Cu (I) species as the active sites for adsorption of CO2 and its intermediates, thereby, promoting further transformation and hydrogenation reactions, while suppressing HER.[9] However, Cu (I) species are not stable during the catalyst preparation and evaluation, which could be easily oxidized to CuO when exposed to air and light, or reduced to Cu under negative applied potential.[7,10] Carbonbased materials have been found to be able to improve the chemical stability of the supported metal oxide species because of their good electron transfer capability and electronic interactions.[11] Moreover, the electronic and catalytic properties of carbon materials could be tuned via the construction of defects, including extrinsic defects and intrinsic defects.[12] The extrinsic defects, such as those produced through heteroatom doping, have been proven to be effective in tuning the electronic properties and catalytic performance of the carbon materials used for catalytic CO2 reduction.[13] The intrinsic carbon defects could also tune the electronic properties of carbon materials, which could form a promising pathway to alter the interaction between the carbon support and active metal.[14] However, the critical roles of intrinsic carbon defects in CO2 reduction are not clearly understood.[15] Recently, 3D vertical graphene (VG) has become an attractive carbon material due to its robust 3D porous structure, surface tailorability, high conductivity, and availability of large-scale preparation methods.[16,17] Thus, defective 3D VG is expected to serve as an efficient platform for investigating the effects of intrinsic carbon defects on the EC CO2 reduction process.
Herein, VG was synthesized on carbon fiber paper (CP) through a plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) method, followed by further modification using a simple postsynthesis Ar-plasma treatment. The Ar-plasma treated VG (VG-Ar) was then employed as the support for Cu nanoparticles
(Cu/VG-Ar) prepared via a galvanostatic pulsed electrodeposition (PED) method (Scheme 1, see also the Experimental Section). As controls, the same method was used to deposit Cu on VG without postsynthesis Ar-plasma treatment (Cu/VG) and commercial 2D graphene paper (Cu/GP). The VG provided abundant anchoring sites for the Cu@CuxO nanoparticles and prevented the aggregation of deposited Cu species as revealed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Furthermore, the postsynthesis Arplasma treatment successfully constructed the intrinsic sp3-type surface defects, confirmed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), Raman spectroscopy, and electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy (EPR). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that the constructed sp3-type carbon defects (originating from carbon adatoms) could stabilize the Cu2O species on VG. Electrochemical measurements demonstrated that the VG-Ar deposited with Cu@CuxO nanoparticles exhibited suppressed HER activity as well as significantly enhanced CO2 reduction performance as compared to Cu/VG and Cu/GP. Cu near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) spectroscopy, XPS, and the in situ synchrotron powder diffraction (PD) experimental results further confirmed the improved stabilization properties of VG-Ar on Cu2O species during catalyst preparation and EC CO2 reduction experiment. Therefore, evidence from experimental and theoretical characterizations, together with performance evaluation revealed that the intrinsic sp3-type carbon defects on Cu/VG-Ar played a vital role in improving the EC CO2 reduction performance of the carbon-supported catalyst.

sections.heading: 2. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
The graphene materials before and after Cu electrodeposition were first characterized using SEM. As illustrated in Figure S1 (Supporting Information), the GP shows a typical 2D layered structure, while the VG and VG-Ar materials exhibit verticallyorientated 3D carbon structures. After the decoration of Cu nanoparticles via PED, the 2D graphene surface was covered by a dense layer of aggregated Cu species. In contrast, the Cu species deposited on VG materials were well-dispersed with the size ranging from 60 to 80  nm. The SEM images of VG and VG-Ar also demonstrate that the postsynthesis Ar-plasma treatment was mild and did not damage the 3D porous structure of VG, which results in the same Cu nanoparticle morphology. This is further confirmed by the TEM images (Figure S2, Supporting Information), demonstrating no obvious changes in the morphology and size of the Cu nanoparticles dispersed on the thin-layer graphene of VG or VG-Ar.
Scheme 1. Schematic illustration for the preparation of Cu/VG-Ar. Surface treatment (ST) using Ar-plasma (RF induced, 13.56 MHz, 1000 W) was used to clean the surface. Plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) was used to grow vertical graphene (VG). Plused galvanostatic electrodeposition (PED, −0.015 A, 1 s pulse, and 7 s delay for 67 cycles) was used to deposit Cu nanoparticles on VG using a Cu aqueous solution (0.02 m CuSO4, 0.15 m lactic acid) as the Cu precursor.

The EC CO2 reduction experiments of the samples were conducted in a three-electrode H-Cell reactor filled with CO2 saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 solution. The total current densities and partial current densities toward CO2 reduction products of Cu/GP, Cu/VG, and Cu/VG-Ar collected at different applied potentials ranging from −0.8 to −1.4 V versus RHE are shown in Figure 1A; and Figure S3 (Supporting Information). The results indicate that the HER was competitive during the electrochemical CO2 reduction experiment, especially for the Cu/GP sample, which exhibits a relatively high total current density but low partial current density toward CO2 reduction products. This means that most of the electrons on Cu/GP were transferred to adsorbed protons and resulted in hydrogen production. In contrast, the increased partial current densities and the improved total FE toward CO2 reduction products over the Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar indicate that the VG supported catalysts possess improved activity and selectivity toward CO2 reduction (Figure 1). Specifically, the maximum FE of Cu/GP for CO2 reduction products is 8.9% with a partial current density of 0.9 mA cm−2 at −1.2 V versus RHE, while Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar exhibit significantly higher values of 26.8% and 60.6% with partial current densities of 2.9 and 5.6  mA  cm−2 under the same conditions, respectively (more details are listed in Table S1, Supporting Information). This suggests 222% and 522% improvements in partial current density for CO2 reduction products compared to that of Cu/GP. In addition, the CO2 reduction product distribution of the Cu/GP, Cu/VG, and Cu/VG-Ar catalysts under different applied potentials (−0.8 to −1.4  V vs RHE) are demonstrated in Figure  1B. At relatively less negative applied potential (−0.8 to −1.0  V vs RHE), the major CO2 reduction products over Cu/GP, Cu/ VG, and Cu/VG-Ar catalysts are carbon monoxide (CO) and formate (HCOO−). As the applied potential increases in negativity (≤ −1.2 V vs RHE), all the catalysts show increased partial current densities for CO2 reduction products, while multicarbon products (ethylene (C2H4), EtOH (CH3CH2OH), and PrOH (CH3CH2CH2OH)) were detected among Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar catalysts (see also Figures S4 and S5, Supporting Information). It has been reported that the CO2 reduction process on the Cu-based catalysts originates from the adsorption and activation of CO2 molecules.[18] The activated CO2 (*CO2•−) would then be converted into HCOO− or CO through a two electron transfer process; the preference of different products depends on how the *CO2•− intermediate is bounded on the Cu surface.[19] Specifically, HCOO− would be produced when CuO bonds are formed between the Cu catalysts and *CO2•−, while CO tends to be the primary products when the *CO2•− is bonded with Cu through CuC bonds. However, CO is not only a final product (like HCOO−), but also a crucial intermediate for the follow-up reactions on the Cu-based catalysts.[20] For instance, CO could be converted into CH4 through protonation reactions,[21] or transformed to C2+ products via the CC coupling mechanisms.[22] The lack of multicarbon products over the Cu/GP catalysts indicates that the generated CO did not readily participate in the protonation and dimerization reactions. This could be due to the relatively low amount of CO attached to the surface of GP catalyst, owing to the planar structure of Cu/GP with limited CO2 anchoring sites and low mass transport capability.[23] Hence, insufficient CO intermediates were present for the protonation and dimerization reactions, leading to the dominant two electron transfer pathways (to generate HCOO− and CO).[24] Moreover, the poor mass transport ability on the 2D Cu/GP could result in the increased adsorption of protons at the expense of CO2 adsorption, causing the Cu/GP catalyst to favor HER and suffer low FE toward CO2 reduction.[25] In contrast, the 3D structure and the resulting nanostructured Cu species of Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar catalysts could improve the CO2 transport to the Cu active sites and enhance the surface CO2 adsorption for the CO2 reduction reaction.[20] The interconnected porous structure of VG may also play an important role in tuning the selectivity toward CO2 reduction. As revealed by the N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms of Cu/GP and Cu/VG (Figure S6, Supporting Information), the VG supported catalyst shows higher surface area and larger pore volume (0.25 m2 cm−2 and 1.9 × 10−3 cm3  cm−2, respectively) compared to those of Cu/GP (0.14 m2  cm−2 and 6.6 × 10−4 cm3  cm−2, respectively).
Figure 1. Electrochemical CO2 reduction performance of Cu/GP, Cu/VG, and Cu/VG-Ar in CO2-saturated 0.1 m KHCO3. A) Total current density (black solid symbols) and partial current density toward CO2 reduction products (blue hollow symbols) under different applied potentials. B) Faradaic efficiency (FE) of main CO2 reduction products over Cu/GP (slash pattern), Cu/VG (cross pattern), and Cu/VG-Ar (blank pattern). GP, VG, and VG-Ar exhibit no CO2 reduction activity under the same experimental conditions.

It is reported that catalysts with porous structures could result in accumulated OH− in the pore interface due to the consumption of protons during the HER reaction, which would cause higher local pH near the catalyst surface, compared with that of catalysts with planar or smooth surfaces. The elevated local pH with reduced proton concentration could then favor the production of multicarbon products.[26] Therefore, the catalytic CO2 reduction performance and the morphological analyses suggest that the unique 3D graphene structure plays an important role in improving the CO2 reduction performance of the catalysts.
Interestingly, despite the similar morphology (Figures S1 and S2, Supporting Information), Cu/VG-Ar demonstrates further improved CO2 reduction performance compared to Cu/VG under different applied potentials (Figure  1, more details are shown in Figures S4 and S5 and Table S1, Supporting Information). Specifically, the Cu/VG-Ar shows higher FE and partial current density toward HCOO− and CO compared with those of Cu/VG under −0.8  V and −1.0  V versus RHE, indicating the enhanced CO2 adsorption and activation capabilities of Cu/VG-Ar, as the CO2 adsorption and activation are the ratedetermining step for the production of HCOO− and CO.[18,27] As the applied potential decreases to −1.2 V versus RHE, the Cu/ VG-Ar catalyst exhibits the highest FE toward CO2 reduction with the partial current densities for HCOO−, C2H4, EtOH, and PrOH increasing significantly by 100%, 155%, 150%, and 200% compared to those of Cu/VG, respectively (Figures S4 and S5, Supporting Information). This means that not only were the CO2 adsorption and activation enhanced, the CC coupling capabilities of Cu/VG-Ar were also improved after the postsynthesis Ar-plasma treatment. Moreover, Cu/VG-Ar shows detectable CH4 products at 1.2 V versus RHE, while Cu/VG starts to produce CH4 at 1.4  V versus RHE. It is reported that the multicarbon products are produced through the CC coupling reaction of *CO intermediates, while CH4 is produced through the protonation of the *CO intermediates. Specifically, the dimerization process is preferred when the *CO mass transport is not limited at lower overpotential, and when the applied potential becomes more negative, the protonation would be preferred when reaching the limit of *CO mass transport.[18,28] However, it should be noted that the *CO intermediate required by both dimerization and protonation processes was generated in the first reaction step from adsorbed *CO2, therefore, the *CO mass transport limiting rate is determined by the *CO2 mass transport limit. Herein, the negligible increase in the total converted CO2 amount from 128.4 to 130.4 µmol when the negative applied potential was increased from −1.2 to −1.4 V versus RHE is due to the reaching of *CO2 mass transport limit in Cu/VG-Ar at −1.2  V versus RHE (Table S1, Supporting Information), which is also signified by the preferred protonation pathway (production of CH4). As such, the CO2 mass transport and adsorption limit of Cu/VG catalyst was reached under applied potential of −1.4  V versus RHE (signified by the production of CH4), which converted 86.1 µmol CO2 (≈34% lower than that of Cu/VG-Ar). This suggests that the Cu/VG-Ar has a better CO2 transport and adsorption capability compared with Cu/VG. In addition, the HER process over the Cu/VG-Ar catalyst was suppressed when compared to that of Cu/VG. For instance, the HER partial current density decreased from
7.8 to 3.7 mA cm−2 at −1.2 V versus RHE after the postsynthesis Ar-plasma treatment (Table S1, Supporting Information). As discussed above, the Ar-plasma treatment of Cu/VG-Ar could enhance the CO2 reduction activity by improving the CO2 adsorption and activation, while promoting the CC coupling reaction and suppressing HER activity.
To understand the excellent CO2 reduction performance of Cu nanoparticles deposited on the VG-Ar support, high-angle annular dark-field aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) and bright field (BF)-STEM were conducted to investigate the crystalline structure and elemental mapping at high resolution. As shown in Figure 2A–C, the VG-Ar shows a typical lattice spacing of graphene (0.34 nm). The deposited Cu nanoparticles consist of different Cu species based on the lattice spacing analysis, which are assigned to Cu (200), Cu (111), Cu2O (110), Cu2O (111), and CuO (111). The energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping (Figure 2D–F) and elemental line profiles (Figure 2G,H) further confirm that the Cu nanoparticle is a hybrid of metallic copper and copper oxides, with metallic Cu as core and Cu oxides on the surface (i.e., Cu@CuxO). The Cu/VG catalyst shows a similar Cu@CuxO morphology as revealed by EDS mapping (Figure S7, Supporting Information).
XPS spectra were also analyzed to investigate the chemical oxidation states of the surface Cu species. The curve fittings of Cu 2p and Cu LMM Auger peaks were conducted according to the reported characteristic features of Cu, Cu2O, and CuO XPS spectra as shown in Figure 3.[29] From the Cu 2p spectra, Cu (II) species can be easily separated from the overlapping Cu (0) and Cu (I) components, while the ratio of Cu (0) and Cu (I) is further confirmed by the curve fitting of the Cu LMM Auger peaks. The curve fitting results (Figure 3A–D) reveal that the surface Cu species on VG-Ar are mainly attributed to Cu2O (92.3%), while metallic Cu and CuO account for 4.4% and 3.3%, respectively. In contrast, the metallic Cu peaks are absent in the XPS spectra of Cu/VG. The proportion of CuO on Cu/VG increases to 26.9%, while the proportion of Cu2O decreases to 73.1% compared to those of Cu/VG-Ar. Figure 3E–H shows the XPS spectra of spent Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar (i.e., after the CO2 reduction). The Cu species on VG demonstrates the disappearance of surface CuO with the corresponding formation of metallic Cu, occupying 27.4% of the Cu species, with the remaining 72.6% of Cu species attributed to Cu2O (0.5% decrease) after the CO2 reduction. For the Cu/VG-Ar sample, the surface Cu2O components are also almost retained during the CO2 reduction experiments (decreased by 1.6%). In contrast, the amount of Cu2O on Cu/GP decreased by 30.0% after the reaction (from 100.0% to 70.0%), as shown in Figure S8 (Supporting Information). This indicates that although the dense structure of Cu2O on Cu/GP could suppress its oxidation during the synthesis and storage,[30] it is not stable under negative applied potential. To this end, it can be shown that the 3D structure of the VG and VG-Ar supports played an important role in stabilizing Cu2O species during the EC CO2 reduction evaluation by promoting electron transfer and reducing electron accumulation,[31] in contrast to the dense layer of Cu2O formed when using the GP support.
In addition to the Cu XPS spectra, NEXAFS spectroscopy was undertaken to further reveal insights of the oxidation states of the Cu species deposited on VG and VG-Ar before and

after the CO2 reduction experiment. As is shown in Figure S9 (Supporting Information), a strong Cu LIII absorption peak ascribed to CuO can be observed at 930.4 eV, while the region at ≈933.1  eV corresponds to Cu2O, with a lower intensity shoulder at 934.6 eV and a weak peak at 937.4 eV indicating the presence of metallic Cu.[32] Qualitatively, these results are consistent to the Cu XPS results, which show a higher peak ratio of Cu2O:CuO on the VG-Ar support. After the CO2 reduction, the CuO peak (at 930.4 eV) decreases significantly for Cu/VG, indicating the reduction of CuO to form Cu (I) or Cu (0). In contrast, only slight changes appear in the spectra after the reaction when the VG-Ar support is used. Similar observations are also made for the Cu LII edge at ≈950  eV. These results therefore corroborate that the VG-Ar support can stabilize the deposited Cu2O species.
To further monitor the chemical and structural evolution in the Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar during the EC CO2 reduction processes, in situ synchrotron PD experiments were conducted to provide better understanding of the active sites and their dynamic changes. The configuration of the in situ synchrotron PD experiments using a custom-built electrochemical cell is shown in Figure S10 (Supporting Information).[33] The electrochemical cell was filled with 2 mL of 0.1 m KHCO3 and purged with CO2 gas during the experiments (see the Experimental Section). The obtained PD patterns of Cu/VG and Cu/ VG-Ar during the 90 min CO2 reduction experiment are shown in Figure 4A,B. Both Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar showed characteristic peaks of Cu2O (002), Cu2O (222), Cu (111), Cu (002), and Cu (002) at 16.0°, 27.8°, 16.3°, 18.8°, and 26.8°, respectively (COD code: 96-900-7498 and 96-710-1265), while only Cu/VG showed a feature of CuO (11-1) at 13.8° (COD code: 96-101-1149). The integrated intensity (peak area) of each characteristic peak was plotted in Figure  4C,D according to the time recorded during the in situ experiments and analyzed using a linear regression method. As shown in Figure  4C, the integrated intensities of Cu (111) phase in Cu/VG obviously increased within the first 60  min, while the CuO (11-1) phase decreased to 0 (or below the detection limit) at the same duration. After the CuO phase disappeared, the intensities of the Cu (111) phase showed negligible change, indicating a direct transformation of the CuO phase into the Cu (111) phase on Cu/VG. Other phases, such as Cu2O (002), Cu2O (222), Cu (002), and Cu (002), changed slightly during the measurement. For Cu/VG-Ar, both Cu2O and Cu phases showed minor changes during the in situ

experiments, as shown in Figure 4D; and Table S2 (Supporting Information). To further study the stability of the Cu species on Cu/VG-Ar, a long-term in situ synchrotron PD experiment (4.0 h) was carried out under the same condition. The characteristic peak integrated intensities of Cu and Cu2O showed limited changes during the 4.0 h measurement (Figure S11, Supporting Information). By computing the T10% (time taken for the peak intensity to be changed by 10%), the linear regression analysis (Table S2, Supporting Information) suggested that the Cu2O species in Cu/VG-Ar samples are relatively stable under EC CO2 reduction reaction (T10% of ≈24 and 14 h for Cu2O (002) and Cu2O (222) phase, respectively). These in situ synchrotron PD results are thus in good agreement with the XPS and NEXAFS results and further confirm the stabilizing effects of the VG-Ar on the deposited Cu2O species. It is worth noting that Cu2O plays an important role in improving EC CO2 reduction performance by favoring the production of multicarbon hydrocarbons due to its strong adsorption of CO2 and related intermediates,[34] whereas CuO is less active for CO2 reduction because of its poor adsorption of CO2 molecules.[35] Moreover, CuO phase was directly reduced to metallic Cu rather than Cu2O as revealed by the in situ synchrotron PD studies in this work. This is consistent with the improved CO2 transport to Cu active sites and enhanced surface CO2 adsorption of Cu/VG-Ar as revealed by the CO2 reduction evaluation experiments. Hence, the superior CO2 reduction performance of Cu/VG-Ar may be attributed to its ability in forming a higher content of surface Cu2O species during its synthesis and maintaining it under reaction conditions. Although there is no obvious morphological difference between Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar, the lowered oxidation states of the surface Cu species indicate that the postsynthesis Arplasma treatment has changed the interaction between defective VG and the deposited Cu nanoparticles. Hence, the C 1s XPS spectra for the Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar samples were analyzed to investigate the changes in bonding configurations of C to Cu. As shown in Figure 5A, both the C1s peaks of the samples were fitted using five states, two of which are attributed to sp2-hybridized carbon (284.6  eV) and sp3-hybridized carbon (285.5  eV).[36,37] The other three states are ascribed to carbon–oxygen groups, i.e., CO (286.7  eV), CO (288.1  eV), and OCO (289.5  eV).[38] The details of the curve fitting results are listed in Table S3 (Supporting Information), which show that the CC bonds in the Cu/VG sample mainly originate from sp2-hybridized carbons (61.7%) in the graphene plane, with 23.2% of carbon bonds attributed to sp3-hybridized carbon. In contrast, the fraction of sp2-hybridized carbon in Cu/VG-Ar decreases to 38.4%, while the fraction of sp3-hybridized carbons increases to 49.3%. Moreover, the percentage of the carbon–oxygen groups does not change significantly (≈2.9% decrease) in Cu/VG-Ar, excluding the possibility of introducing oxygen functional groups into the VG surface by postsynthesis Ar plasma treatment. Therefore, the effect of oxygen functional groups in altering catalytic performance could be eliminated. The Raman spectra of Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar show two main distinct peaks (Figure 5B), which could be ascribed to the G band (1585 cm−1) and D band (1350 cm−1) characteristics of graphene materials, respectively. in-plane vibration of sp2-bonded carbons, while the D band is attributed to the breathing vibration of sp2-carbons activated by neighboring defects.[16,39] It is found that the intensity ratio of the D and G band (ID/IG) increases in the Cu/VG-Ar sample (ID/IG  = 1.50) compared to that of Cu/VG (ID/IG  = 1.30), suggesting an increased level of surface defects in the graphene plane after Ar-plasma treatment. The D′ band at ≈1623 cm−1 in the Cu/VG sample corresponds to the defect-induced intravalley double-resonance scattering process, which could be distinguished from the G band at a moderate concentration of defects or disorders in graphene; while it would merge with the G band at a high defect concentration.[36,40] Hence, the disappearance of the D’ band and the broader G band in the Raman spectrum of the Cu/VG-Ar also suggest the high defect concentration in Cu/VG-Ar, which is consistent with the C1s XPS results. In addition, the peaks with Raman shift under 700 cm−1 are from the surface Cu oxides deposited on the graphene material. Both Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar show characteristic peaks of Cu2O at 150, 220, 415, 520, and 630 cm−1. The absence of characteristic peaks of CuO (300, 348, and 633 cm−1) and Cu(OH)2 (290 and 490 cm−1) indicates that the Cu oxides species deposited on the VG materials are mainly Cu2O,[41] which further confirms the findings in the Cu 2p and Cu LMM XPS spectra.
The C1s XPS spectra and Raman spectra reveal an increase of surface defects in the VG-Ar with the formation of sp3hybridized carbons. As foreign adatom defects could be excluded because there were no other elements introduced during the postsynthesis Ar-plasma treatment (Figure S12, Supporting Information), the sp3-hybridized defects could be attributed to intrinsic graphene defects, such as edge defects and/or carbon adatoms.[12] EPR spectra of VG and VG-Ar were further analyzed to identify the sp3-defect types during the Ar-plasma treatment. In Figure  5C, the VG exhibits a broad EPR band derived from the spins of free unpaired electrons in extended π-electron systems of graphene edges.[42,43] As compared to VG, the g-value of the free electrons in VG-Ar slightly decreases from 2.0050 to 2.0044 (Table S4, Supporting Information), indicating a decrease in spin–orbit interaction or exchange interaction of VG-Ar.[44] Since the spin–orbit interaction between carbon atoms is negligible compared to the evident exchange interaction in graphene, the decrease of g-value in VG-Ar could be attributed to the reduced exchange interaction resulted from weaker wave function overlap between the unpaired electrons.[45] This indicates that the distance between unpaired electrons is increased due to the decreased amount of unpaired electrons.[46] In addition to the qualitative analysis of EPR spectra, semiquantitative EPR analysis was also conducted using 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) as reference (Figure S13, Supporting Information). The EPR spectra of VG materials were doubly integrated and compared with the double integration of the DPPH reference spectrum (which possessed 1.40 × 108 spins) to calculate the spin density (Table S5, Supporting Information). The spin densities of VG-Ar decrease by 13.6% when compared to VG, suggesting the loss of unpaired electrons during the postsynthesis Ar-plasma treatment, which is consistent with the changes in the g-value. The changed electronic properties due to the constructed defects can be responsible for the lowered oxidation states of the deposited Cu species. Mott–Schottky spectra show that the charge carrier density in VG-Ar increases by 69.6% compared to VG (Figure  5D),[49] indicating that the constructed defects may lead to carbon self-doping effects in VG-Ar.[45,50] Hence, the increased electron densities near the defects can act as an electron source to minimize Cu oxidation of the deposited Cu nanoparticles.[51] To further understand the mechanism, DFT calculations of the Cu oxidation energy barrier were performed on a conventional graphene and a defective graphene layer with carbon adatoms. Cu12O6 (Cu2O) was modeled as the initial Cu species on a graphene layer. A 5  ×  5 graphene super cell was employed to simulate the interaction of Cu12Ox clusters (x = 6, 7, 8, 9, 10) with different carbon structures and thus the energetics of the Cu12O6 (Cu2O) oxidation process could be studied. Particularly, the effects of sp3 carbons introduced by the postsynthesis Ar-plasma treatment were studied and compared to the sp2 carbons. The different carbon structures used for simulation are shown in Figure 5E, where the distortion of the graphene layer was caused by the sp2/sp3 composite structure.[52]

The Bader analysis on different carbon structures shows that sp3 carbons localize more electrons (0.02 e), which could explain the increased electron density in VG-Ar as detected by Mott–Schottky spectra. The sp2 carbons seemed to favor the oxidation process of the Cu12O6 cluster. This is clear from the calculated potential energy diagrams, which show that the process of Cu2O oxidation is energetically more downhill (more favorable) on the planar sp2 carbons than on the sp3 carbons (Figure 5F), especially for the addition of the first oxygen atoms (oxidation is more favorable on sp2 carbons by 4.43 eV). These results suggest that the oxidation of Cu species is less favorable on configurations containing sp3 carbons than those on sp2 carbons. Accordingly, the defective VG-Ar which has more sp3 carbons impeded the deposited Cu nanoparticles from excessive oxidation and maintained the Cu oxidation states. This is consistent with the experimental XPS and NEXAFS analysis (Figure  3; and Figure S9, Supporting Information) which demon strate more Cu(I) species in Cu/VG-Ar when compared to Cu/VG (92.3% and 73.1%, respectively), and less Cu(II) species in Cu/VG-Ar when compared to Cu/VG (3.3% and 26.9%, respectively). The increased ratio of sp3 carbons does not only enhance the CO2 adsorption abilities by lowering the Cu oxidation states, but also adsorb more CO2 compared to sp2 carbons as previously reported.[53]
To further confirm that the defective VG-Ar plays a critical role in improving the CO2 reduction performance, the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves of the VG and VG-Ar (both without Cu) were measured in the same H-cell used in the CO2 reduction evaluation, which was filled with CO2 saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 solution. As VG and VG-Ar show no activity for CO2 reduction, their LSV curves (Figure 6A) are attributed to HER activity. Hence, the decreased current density of the VG-Ar shows the suppression of HER compared with VG. Furthermore, the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted to study the plasma-induced changes in electron transfer resistance. The Nyquist plots (Figure 6B) show the difference in the charge transfer and diffusion behavior of VG and VG-Ar, which was interpreted by the inserted equivalent circuit model (simulation details shown in Table S5, Supporting Information). Specifically, the electrode and electrolyte resistance (R1) slightly increases to 17.1 Ω after Ar-plasma treatment
compared to VG at 16.2 Ω, which could be attributed to the increased electrical resistance caused by higher sp3-hybridized carbon content.[54] Besides, the charge transfer resistance (Rct) is comprised of the resistance between the CP and VG (R2) together with the resistance between the VG and electrolyte (R3), which also increased after the Ar-plasma treatment (from 22.9 to 26.9 Ω for VG and VG-Ar, respectively). Moreover, the diffusion layer resistance R4 of the Warburg impedance (Zw) obviously increases from 48.1 Ω for VG to 72.9 Ω for VG-Ar sample, indicating that the introduction of sp3 carbons in graphene material could limit the electron transfer and diffusion to adsorbed protons. Therefore, the resulting higher resistance in electron transfer and diffusion can explain the suppressed HER activity of VG-Ar.[55] The electrochemical properties of the VG-Ar investigated by the LSV and EIS spectra reveal that the constructed defects suppressed the HER activity of the VG-Ar material mainly through increasing direct charge transfer resistance and diffusion resistance between VG-Ar and electrolyte. The increased charge transfer and diffusion resistance could also change the electron transfer pathway during the CO2 reduction evaluation. Specifically, the electron transfer pathway from the VG-Ar, via the deposited Cu@CuxO, to the adsorbed CO2 could be preferred rather than from VG-Ar directly to the protons in electrolyte, which is consistent with the improved CO2 reduction activity and suppressed HER side reactions as shown in Figure  1. Therefore, it could be concluded that both the defective VG-Ar and stabilized Cu@CuxO are responsible for improving the CO2 adsorption capability of the catalyst, by channeling the electrons toward the surface adsorbed CO2. This work highlights the crucial roles of the intrinsic sp3-type defects in the modification of VG and its interactions with deposited catalyst, which could serve as primary evidence that the Ar-plasma treatment could help to tune the performance and selectivity of carbon-based electrocatalysts.

sections.heading: 3. Conclusion
sections.text:
Through a scalable plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition method, Cu nanoparticles deposited on 3D defective vertical graphene electrocatalyts have been successfully synthesized
Adv. Funct. Mater. 2020, 1910118
1910118 (10 of 12) © 2020 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim
for the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction. As compared to traditional 2D graphene supported catalysts, the unique 3D structures of VG provided the Cu species with more anchoring sites, thus giving better Cu dispersion. In addition, the Arplasma treatment generated intrinsic sp3-type graphene defects without damaging the structure of the 3D graphene. The defective vertical graphene with high surface electron density and tuned interaction with deposited Cu species were shown to promote the formation of active Cu (I) species and have a stabilizing effect during reaction conditions. The abundant presence of Cu2O on the catalyst surface enhanced the CO2 adsorption and reaction primarily to various liquid hydrocarbon products. In addition, the presence of surface defects suppressed HER activity by channeling electrons to Cu-based active sites. The reported VG materials and intrinsic defect construction methods herein open a new pathway for the design of carbon supported metal catalysts to achieve superior electrochemical performance, using industrially available synthesis methods.

sections.heading: 4. Experimental Section
sections.text:
Material Synthesis: Synthesis of VG-Ar and VG: VG-Ar and VG were prepared via a PECVD method. In the first step, commercial carbon fiber paper (CP, Toray 060) was treated by an RF induced Ar-plasma (10 sccm Ar flow, 13.56 MHz, 1000 W) and employed as the substrate for follow-up growth of VG. Afterward, H2 and CH4 (10 sccm each) were introduced into the chamber as the precursor of VG. Then, VG grew under plasma irradiation for 10 min before the chamber was evacuated again to eliminate all of the gas precursors. Next, Ar-plasma was reignited to treat the synthesized VG for another 1  min to obtain the VG-Ar. Commercial graphene paper (GP, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as a control support.
Synthesis of Cu/VG-Ar, Cu/VG, and Cu/GP: The Cu/VG-Ar, Cu/VG, and Cu/GP were prepared through a galvanostatic PED method. The Cu precursor used for PED was prepared by CuSO4∙5H2O (0.02 m, SigmaAldrich, 98%) and latic acid (0.15 m, Sigma-Aldrich, 90%), the pH of which was adjusted to 7.0 by NaOH solution (Saturated, Sigma-Aldrich, 98%). VG-Ar, VG, and GP were used as working electrode in a threeelectrode system connected to an Autolab potentiostat (PGSTAT204) for the Cu deposition (Pt foil as counter electrode and Ag/AgCl electrode as reference electrode). All PED pulses were 1s in length (−0.015 A) with a 7 s delay (0 A), 67 pulses were conducted to control the Cu deposition amount.
Characterization Methods: SEM was undertaken using a FEI Nova NanoSEM 450. TEM was undertaken using a Phillips CM200. The BFand HAADF-STEM were collected using JEOL JEM-ARM200F STEM. XPS was measured using SAGE 150 SPECS with Mg Kα source (1253.6  eV). Raman spectroscopy was collected from an inVia Raman spectrometer with 514 nm Argon ion laser. EPR was collected using Bruker EMX X-Band ESR Spectrometer. EPR spectra were obtained under 120 K and then normalized based on the weight of the samples used for measurement. Electrochemical characterizations, such as Mott–Schottky spectroscopy (frequency of 10  kHz), LSV, and EIS were performed in 0.1 m KHCO3 with an Autolab potentiostat (PGSTAT204). NEXAFS spectroscopy measurements were performed at the soft X-ray (SXR) beamline of the Australian Synchrotron to probe the Cu LIII and LII-edges.[56] For NEXAFS, Cu/VG and Cu/VG-Ar, as well as their spent analogs were directly adhered to the sample holder using carbon tape. All NEXAFS data reduction and processing was performed using the program QANT.[57]
Computational Methods: DFT Calculations: To simulate the interaction of different Cu12Ox clusters with the carbon structures, ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations were employed.[58] These calculations were carried out using the plane-wave DFT code, VASP.[59] The projector augmented wave (PAW) method was used to treat the
core electrons,[60] and the exchange-correlation functional was set to Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof.[61] The wavefunctions were expanded with a kinetic energy cut-off value of 450 eV and a gamma point k-grid was used. A vacuum region greater than 10 Å in the direction normal to the graphene plane was used to avoid interactions between periodic images. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out using the canonical ensemble (NVT, amount of substance (N), volume (V), temperature (T)) using a Nose–Hoover thermostat set to 310 K. A timestep of 1 fs was used and the simulations were carried out for 1 ps. The total energy of the system was taken to be the average of the final 500 steps of the MD run. The favorability of oxidation (addition of oxygen atoms to Cu12O6) on different carbon structures was assessed using the equation E E E En
n /2O Cu O Cu O O12 6 12 6 2∆ = − −+ , where n = 1, 2, 3, and 4.
Electrochemical CO2 Reduction Experiments: The electrochemical CO2 reduction experiments of prepared catalysts were conducted in a threeelectrode H-Cell reactor filled with CO2 saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 solution (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.7%). The synthesized Cu/graphene catalyst was used as working electrode, while Pt foil and Ag/AgCl electrode were used as counter and reference electrode, respectively. The working electrode and counter electrode were seperated by a Nafion 117 membrane (Dupont) and connected to Autolab potentiostat (PGSTAT204). Each sample was evaluated for 1.5 h before the gas phase products were collected for analysis using gas chromatography (GC-2010, Shimadzu) and the liquid phase products were analyzed by nuclear magnetic resonance (Avance III 600 MHz NMR, Bruker) using a presaturation method for water suppression.
In Situ Synchrotron PD Experiment: In situ synchrotron PD data were collected using a three-electrode electrochemical cell equipped with Ag/ AgCl electrode as reference electrode, Pt wire as counter electrode, and the prepared Cu-based electrode as working electrode. The customdesigned electrochemical cell was the modified version of cell reported in a previous in operando photoelectrochemical experiment.[33] The cell has a Kapton window of 2  cm in diameter and cell width of 0.5  cm. During the measurements, the cell was filled with 2 mL of 0.1 m KHCO3 and purged with CO2 gas under −1.2 V versus RHE for 1.5 h during the data collection. The detailed configuration of the in situ synchrotron PD electrochemical cell is shown in Figure S10 (Supporting Information). The in situ data were collected on the PD beamline at the Australian Synchrotron Facility, Melbourne, Victoria at X-ray wavelength of 0.59 Å.[62] Each data set was collected for 6 min in transmission geometry throughout the cell during the 1.5 h of electrochemical reaction. The long-term in situ synchrotron PD experiments were conducted for 4.0 h under the same condition.
